claims.source: This confirms that signal amplitude is not limited by 11S (see also below) and is a faithful measure of imported PCP, irrespective of how much is added to the outside.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data showing no correlation between 11S concentration and signal amplitude (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C).

claims.claim: 11S is correctly localised in the matrix and not the IMS.
claims.source: Thus, we can conclude that 11S is correctly localised in the matrix and not the IMS.
claims.evidence: This is supported by digitonin extraction experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Signal amplitude is linearly related to PCP concentration from 753 fM up to ~45 nM, where it plateaus.
claims.source: Plotting the results shows that amplitude is linearly related to PCP concentration from 753 fM up to ~45 nM, where it plateaus (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Only a tiny fraction of the PCP added reaches the matrix.
claims.source: Evidently then, only a tiny fraction of the PCP added reaches the matrix.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the calculation that if all 45 nM PCP were imported, it would correspond to roughly 540 µM inside the matrix, which exceeds the internal 11S concentration.

claims.claim: When DHFR is positioned C-terminal to pep86 with sufficient length between the two to span the TOM and TIM complexes, import signal is observed in the presence of MTX.
claims.source: However, when DHFR is positioned C-terminal to pep86 (PCP-pep86-DHFR) with sufficient length between the two to span the TOM and TIM complexes (212 amino acids in this case, longer than the 135 required [Rassow et al., 1989]), we do see an import signal (Figure 2A, orange bars).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: NanoLuc can form as soon as pep86 enters the matrix and does not require the entire PCP to be imported.
claims.source: This confirms that NanoLuc can form as soon as pep86 enters the matrix and does not require the entire PCP to be imported, as seen previously with the bacterial Sec system (Allen et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the experimental data with PCP-pep86-DHFR and comparison to previous work.

claims.claim: The presence or absence of MTX makes only a minor difference to the amplitude of the signal for PCP-pep86-DHFR.
claims.source: Importantly, the presence or absence of MTX makes only a minor difference to the amplitude of this signal (Figure 2A, orange bars).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Only about 20% of the signal arises from turnovers beyond the first one.
claims.source: The slope, which corresponds to the increase in amplitude per 1 nM PCP-pep86-DHFR, is 1.22 times greater in the absence of MTX, meaning only about 20% of the signal arises from turnovers beyond the first one.
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Import behaves as single turnover under the restrictive conditions using isolated mitochondria.
claims.source: Of course, while this does not mean that import is strictly single turnover – which would certainly seem implausible for fully functional mitochondria in their native environment – it does suggest that it behaves as single turnover under the restrictive conditions here, using isolated mitochondria (without the cytosol).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing minimal difference in amplitude with and without MTX.

claims.claim: The amount of PCP-pep86-DHFR that was fully internalised in the matrix in the absence of MTX (11 pmol per mg mitochondria) matched closely the approximate amount of TIM23 dimer estimated to be in the sample of mitochondria (8.5 pmol per mg mitochondrial protein).
claims.source: Consistent with this interpretation, the amount of PCP-pep86-DHFR that was fully internalised in the matrix in the absence of MTX (11 pmol per mg mitochondria, based on quantification of Western blot bands in Figure 2—figure supplement 1) matched closely the approximate amount of TIM23 dimer estimated to be in the sample of mitochondria (8.5 pmol per mg mitochondrial protein [Sirrenberg et al., 1997]).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot quantification data and comparison to published values.

claims.claim: Signal amplitude can be reduced by depleting ∆ψ.
claims.source: It has previously been shown that signal amplitude can be reduced by depleting ∆ψ (Pereira et al., 2019), which would suggest that available energy limits protein import.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data from a previous study.

claims.claim: Available energy limits protein import.
claims.source: It has previously been shown that signal amplitude can be reduced by depleting ∆ψ (Pereira et al., 2019), which would suggest that available energy limits protein import.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that depleting ∆ψ reduces signal amplitude.

claims.claim: 'Resetting' the channel after import possibly requires dimerisation of TIM23.
claims.source: This can be reconciled with the apparent single turnover nature of the reaction if 'resetting' the channel after import – possibly through dimerisation of TIM23, as previously reported (Bauer et al., 1996) – requires additional energy input.
claims.evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on previous reports of TIM23 dimerisation.

claims.claim: Formation of NanoLuc is faster than about 5 min⁻¹ and will not be resolved in the experimental setup.
claims.source: It is also important to note that any additional step faster than about 5 min–1 will not be resolved in our experimental set up – due to the limitations of the plate reader (see detailed explanation in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A). Instead, the extra step will manifest itself as a small apparent additional lag before the signal appears (equal to 1/kstep, where kstep is the rate constant for that process; Allen et al., 2020). This includes formation of NanoLuc: it is >7.4 min–1 even at the lowest estimated 11S concentration, as determined in solution (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data and technical limitations of the measurement system.

claims.claim: Import kinetics are not appreciably affected by the concentration of matrix 11S.
claims.source: Consistent with this, we observe that the import kinetics are not appreciably affected by the concentration of matrix 11S, despite its variance (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claims.claim: k1′ corresponds to transport of the PCP through TOM.
claims.source: However, as detailed below, they can be distinguished by perturbing the system and seeing how this affects the different rates. From this, and based on the results in the following sections, we assign k1′ as transport of the PCP through TOM and k2′ as subsequent engagement of the MTS with the TIM23 complex.
claims.evidence: This assignment is based on experimental data from perturbation experiments and analysis of length and position variants.

claims.claim: k2′ corresponds to subsequent engagement of the MTS with the TIM23 complex.
claims.source: However, as detailed below, they can be distinguished by perturbing the system and seeing how this affects the different rates. From this, and based on the results in the following sections, we assign k1′ as transport of the PCP through TOM and k2′ as subsequent engagement of the MTS with the TIM23 complex.
claims.evidence: This assignment is based on experimental data from perturbation experiments and analysis of length and position variants.

claims.claim: There is no significant difference between any of the four position variants with respect to amplitude, k1′, or k2′.
claims.source: We observe no significant difference between any of the four position variants with respect to any of the three parameters, indicating that transport through TIM23 is fast, and not rate-limiting; therefore, it does not contribute appreciably to the kinetics of import.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claims.claim: Transport through TIM23 is fast and not rate-limiting.
claims.source: We observe no significant difference between any of the four position variants with respect to any of the three parameters, indicating that transport through TIM23 is fast, and not rate-limiting; therefore, it does not contribute appreciably to the kinetics of import.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the lack of difference between position variants.

claims.claim: Signal amplitude is inversely correlated with protein length for the length variant series.
claims.source: For the length series, signal amplitude is inversely correlated with protein length (Figure 3C, left panel in orange).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Shorter proteins are able to accumulate at higher levels in the matrix compared to large ones.
claims.source: The only plausible explanation is that shorter proteins are able to accumulate at higher levels in the matrix compared to large ones.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that amplitude varies with protein length but not with pep86 position.

claims.claim: k1′ has a strong inverse correlation with PCP length.
claims.source: Strikingly, we find that k1ʹ has a strong inverse correlation with PCP length (but not pep86 position), i.e., it is faster for smaller proteins (Figure 3C, middle graph).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The step time (1/k1′) increases exponentially as a function of PCP length.
claims.source: Even more surprisingly, the corresponding step time (1/k1ʹ) increases not linearly but exponentially as a function of PCP length (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Exponential length-dependence is characteristic of an unbiased reversible diffusion-based (passive) mechanism.
claims.source: Exponential length-dependence is not a characteristic of a powered or biased directional transport, such as we have seen previously for the Sec system (Allen et al., 2020), but rather an unbiased reversible diffusion-based (passive) mechanism (Simon et al., 1992).
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge about transport mechanisms and comparison to previous work.

claims.claim: All three parameters (amplitude, k1′, and k2′) show a dependence on PCP concentration for the length series.
claims.source: Unexpectedly, all three parameters show a dependence on [PCP] for the length series.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The apparent KMs for k1′ are in the low 100s of nM and not systematically dependent on PCP length.
claims.source: The apparent KMs for k1ʹ, (Figure 3E, teal) are in the low 100 s of nM and not systematically dependent on PCP length – this is reasonable for initial association of PCP with TOM.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: The Kds for amplitude and KMs for k2′ are very similar to one another and increase with increasing PCP length.
claims.source: The Kds for amplitude and KMs for k2ʹ, meanwhile (magenta and brown, respectively in Figure 3E), are very similar to one another: they are very low (high affinity) but increase (decrease in affinity) with increasing PCP length.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: Amplitude and k2′ reflect the same process, i.e., the final kinetic step of transport.
claims.source: Because amplitude and k2′ behave identically, it seems reasonable to assume that they reflect the same process, i.e., the final kinetic step of transport (because amplitude is, by definition, successful transport).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the similar concentration dependence of amplitude and k2′.

claims.claim: There is no systematic difference between the position variants in terms of concentration dependence.
claims.source: Just as before, we find no systematic difference between the position variants (Figure 3F) – again suggesting that passage of the PCP through TIM23 is not limiting the overall import rate.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: 10 nM of valinomycin is sufficient to substantially reduce ∆ψ without completely abolishing precursor transport.
claims.source: Mitochondria were pre-treated with valinomycin, a potassium ionophore, which depletes membrane potential in the presence of K+ ions: 10 nM of valinomycin was used – sufficient to substantially reduce ∆ψ (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) without completely abolishing precursor transport (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claims.claim: The effect of valinomycin on signal amplitude is roughly the same for all length and position variants.
claims.source: The effect on the signal amplitude is roughly the same for all length and position variants (Figure 4A, left panel) – in contrast to both apparent rate constants: k1ʹ is somewhat slowed for shorter proteins but largely unaffected for longer ones (Figure 4A, middle panel), while k2ʹ is somewhat slowed for short proteins but dramatically reduced for longer ones (Figure 4A, right panel).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: k1′ is somewhat slowed by valinomycin for shorter proteins but largely unaffected for longer ones.
claims.source: The effect on the signal amplitude is roughly the same for all length and position variants (Figure 4A, left panel) – in contrast to both apparent rate constants: k1ʹ is somewhat slowed for shorter proteins but largely unaffected for longer ones (Figure 4A, middle panel), while k2ʹ is somewhat slowed for short proteins but dramatically reduced for longer ones (Figure 4A, right panel).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: k2′ is somewhat slowed by valinomycin for short proteins but dramatically reduced for longer ones.
claims.source: The effect on the signal amplitude is roughly the same for all length and position variants (Figure 4A, left panel) – in contrast to both apparent rate constants: k1ʹ is somewhat slowed for shorter proteins but largely unaffected for longer ones (Figure 4A, middle panel), while k2ʹ is somewhat slowed for short proteins but dramatically reduced for longer ones (Figure 4A, right panel).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Endogenous matrix ATP under conditions of ATP depletion is minimal.
claims.source: Endogenous matrix ATP under these conditions is minimal, as is evident from the fact that import becomes highly sensitive to antimycin A, an inhibitor of oxidative phosphorylation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing sensitivity to antimycin A.

claims.claim: ATP depletion shows reduced amplitude, with this effect being more pronounced for longer PCPs.
claims.source: Import experiments performed with depleted ATP show reduced amplitude, but unlike the response to valinomycin, this effect is more pronounced for the longer PCPs (Figure 4B, left panel) – consistent with the proposed role for ATP in promoting transport of the mature part of the PCP.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: ATP depletion has little or no effect on k1′.
claims.source: ATP depletion has little or no effect on k1ʹ (Figure 4B, middle panel) and a relatively minor effect on k2ʹ (Figure 4B, right panel), affecting both the length and position variants roughly equally.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: ATP depletion has a relatively minor effect on k2′.
claims.source: ATP depletion has little or no effect on k1ʹ (Figure 4B, middle panel) and a relatively minor effect on k2ʹ (Figure 4B, right panel), affecting both the length and position variants roughly equally.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The concentration dependence of k1′ saturates with an apparent KM of around 100–200 nM.
claims.source: Based on its dependence on PCP concentration (Figure 3E; Figure 3—figure supplement 1), we assign k1ʹ to the initial interaction between PCP and TOM. However, the concentration dependence of this step saturates with an apparent KM of around 100–200 nM.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Under the experimental conditions, the entire PCP passes through TOM before transport through TIM23 is initiated.
claims.source: The strong dependence of k1ʹ on PCP length (Figure 3C, middle panel) provides a clue as to the nature of k1 – it is likely to correspond to passage of the PCP across the OMM, through the TOM complex. The non-linear dependence of step time (1/k1ʹ) on PCP length (Figure 3D) also suggests that this step is at least partially diffusional rather than driven by an active energy-dependent directional motor. Furthermore, it suggests that, under these experimental conditions at least, the entire PCP passes through TOM before transport through TIM23 is initiated.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the exponential length-dependence of k1′.

claims.claim: k2′ is primarily the ∆ψ-dependent insertion of the pre-sequence through TIM23, not the subsequent passage of the unfolded passenger domain.
claims.source: Since k2ʹ shows very little dependence on PCP length in energised mitochondria (Figure 3C, right panel), we propose that it is primarily the ∆ψ-dependent insertion of the pre-sequence through TIM23, not the subsequent passage of the unfolded passenger domain that is limiting (although both presumably contribute to the apparent rate constant).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the lack of length-dependence of k2′ in energised mitochondria.

claims.claim: Under conditions of ∆ψ depletion, a length-dependence of k2′ emerges.
claims.source: However, under conditions of ∆ψ depletion, a length-dependence of k2ʹ emerges (Figure 4A, right panel, orange open circles).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: ∆ψ drives the transport of the mature domain of the precursor, and not exclusively the MTS.
claims.source: This suggests that ∆ψ drives the transport of the mature domain of the precursor, and not exclusively the MTS, and is consistent with the import rate of the rest of the PCP being affected by (∆ψ [Schendzielorz et al., 2017], and see also below).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the emergence of length-dependence of k2′ under ∆ψ depletion and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Removal of the OMM should eliminate steps at the OMM (k1) but not at the IMM (k2).
claims.source: To confirm our assignments of k1ʹ and k2ʹ, we tested the effect of removing the OMM (producing mitoplasts) on import kinetics. If the model is correct, this should eliminate steps at the OMM (i.e. k1) but not at the IMM (k2).
claims.evidence: This is a prediction based on the proposed model.

claims.claim: Mitoplasts were isolated from yeast mitochondria using an optimised concentration of 2 mg/ml digitonin.
claims.source: Mitoplasts were isolated from yeast mitochondria using an optimised concentration of 2 mg/ml digitonin, and successful removal of the OMM was confirmed by respirometry (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the experimental method used.

claims.claim: Even without the OMM, a two-step model is required to describe the data.
claims.source: Even without the OMM, a two-step model is required to describe the data; however, while the values for k2ʹ are similar in mitoplasts to those observed in mitochondria (Figure 5), k1ʹ is substantially increased by removal of the OMM for both the shortest (Figure 5A) and longest (Figure 5B) of the length variant PCPs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: k2′ is unaffected by removal of the OMM, confirming that it takes place at the IMM.
claims.source: The fact that k2' is unaffected by removal of the OMM confirms that it takes place at the IMM, as predicted.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing mitochondria and mitoplasts.

claims.claim: k1′ is substantially increased by removal of the OMM.
claims.source: Even without the OMM, a two-step model is required to describe the data; however, while the values for k2ʹ are similar in mitoplasts to those observed in mitochondria (Figure 5), k1ʹ is substantially increased by removal of the OMM for both the shortest (Figure 5A) and longest (Figure 5B) of the length variant PCPs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claims.claim: Signal amplitude is almost completely unaffected by OMM removal for the shortest protein (L).
claims.source: For the shortest protein, L, signal amplitude is almost completely unaffected by OMM removal, while for the longest, DDDL, amplitude is only moderately reduced (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: The reduction in amplitude for the longest protein (DDDL) in mitoplasts is most likely due to a slightly depleted ∆ψ.
claims.source: For the shortest protein, L, signal amplitude is almost completely unaffected by OMM removal, while for the longest, DDDL, amplitude is only moderately reduced (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C). Most likely, the latter reduction is due to a slightly depleted ∆ψ in mitoplasts.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that amplitude is reduced for longer proteins in mitoplasts.

claims.claim: Amplitude is strongly inversely correlated with net charge of the PCP.
claims.source: The most immediately striking observation is that amplitude is strongly inversely correlated with net charge of the PCP – the opposite of what might be expected given the direction of ∆ψ (inside negative; Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: PCPs cause strong depolarisation of ∆ψ, and this effect diminishes with increasing net negative charge.
claims.source: The PCPs did indeed cause strong depolarisation of ∆ψ, and moreover, this effect diminished with increasing net negative charge.
claims.evidence: This is supported by TMRM fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: Pre-treatment of mitochondria with valinomycin abolishes the correlation between net charge and amplitude.
claims.source: A second prediction from the above hypothesis is that membrane depolarisation prior to protein import will abolish the correlation between net charge and amplitude. This is indeed exactly what we observe: pre-treatment of mitochondria with valinomycin reduces amplitudes for all PCPs, but the effect is greater for more negatively charged PCPs, bringing all amplitudes to about the same level (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: Depleting ATP has very little effect on amplitude for the charge variant PCPs.
claims.source: Depleting ATP, meanwhile, has very little effect on amplitude, just as for the Acp1-based PCPs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: Positively charged PCPs are imported much faster than negatively charged ones.
claims.source: It is clear from looking directly at the import traces that positively charged PCPs are imported much faster than negatively charged ones (albeit reaching a lower final amplitude; Figure 6B–C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claims.claim: The more positively charged PCPs do not show the characteristic delay before signal appears that indicates a two-step transport model.
claims.source: Furthermore, the more positively charged PCPs do not show the characteristic delay before signal appears that indicates a two-step transport model (see Figure 1C); in this case a simpler single-step model is sufficient.
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis of the import traces for positively charged PCPs.

claims.claim: Higher amplitudes are observed for shorter and more negatively charged native PCPs.
claims.source: Consistent with our earlier results, we see higher amplitudes for the shorter and more negatively charged PCPs (Figure 7B), and faster import of the shorter PCPs than the longer ones (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Faster import is observed for shorter native PCPs than longer ones.
claims.source: Consistent with our earlier results, we see higher amplitudes for the shorter and more negatively charged PCPs (Figure 7B), and faster import of the shorter PCPs than the longer ones (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: The effect of net charge on import rate holds true for larger native PCPs.
claims.source: The effect of net charge seen above – faster rates for positively charged PCPs – holds true for the larger PCPs (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Two major distinct events are responsible for the majority of the PCP transit time: passage of the PCP through the TOM complex and insertion of the pre-sequence through the TIM23MOTOR complex.
claims.source: Our results suggest that two major distinct events are responsible for the majority of the PCP transit time: passage of the PCP through the TOM complex and insertion of the pre-sequence through the TIM23MOTOR complex.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion based on all the experimental data presented.

claims.claim: The initial binding of PCP to TOM is fairly rapid.
claims.source: By contrast, the initial binding of PCP to TOM is fairly rapid, as is passage of the mature PCP domain through TIM23.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic analysis showing that these steps are not rate-limiting.

claims.claim: Passage of the mature PCP domain through TIM23 is fairly rapid.
claims.source: By contrast, the initial binding of PCP to TOM is fairly rapid, as is passage of the mature PCP domain through TIM23.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect of pep86 position on import kinetics.

claims.claim: Import appears to be largely single turnover under the experimental conditions.
claims.source: Import appears to be largely single turnover under our experimental conditions, i.e., each import site only imports a single PCP.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the MTX blocking experiments and comparison of imported PCP amounts to TIM23 levels.

claims.claim: Under experimental conditions, import is limited by the amount of energy available in the form of ∆ψ.
claims.source: We propose that, under experimental conditions, import is limited by the amount of energy available in the form of ∆ψ.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that import causes depolarisation that is not restored and that amplitude is affected by ∆ψ depletion.

claims.claim: PCP import causes a depolarisation of the IMM that is not restored.
claims.source: Indeed, measurements of ∆ψ using TMRM confirm that PCP import causes a depolarisation of the IMM that is not restored.
claims.evidence: This is supported by TMRM fluorescence measurements.

claims.claim: PCPs that require more total energy to import (such as longer ones) or that are likely to consume more ∆ψ (positively charged ones) reach a lower final concentration in the mitochondrial matrix at saturating PCP concentrations.
claims.source: Also consistent with ∆ψ being consumed, we find that the PCPs that require more total energy to import (such as longer ones) or that are likely to consume more ∆ψ (positively charged ones) reach a lower final concentration in the mitochondrial matrix at saturating PCP concentrations.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing effects of length and charge on amplitude.

claims.claim: The isolated mitochondria are capable of building a PMF via respiration.
claims.source: Importantly, we were able to show that the IMM depolarisation is an effect of import rather than an inherent problem with the mitochondria preparation. The isolated mitochondria are indeed capable of building a PMF via respiration (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and Figure 6—figure supplement 2), and furthermore, recovering PMF after dissipation caused by externally added ADP (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by respirometry data.

claims.claim: The sustained dissipation of ∆ψ is a consequence of the import process due to charge associated with the PCP itself and/or co-transporting ions.
claims.source: Therefore, the sustained dissipation of ∆ψ must be a consequence of the import process due to charge associated with the PCP itself and/or co-transporting ions.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mitochondria can build and recover PMF, but import causes sustained depolarisation.

claims.claim: With sub-saturating levels of precursor proteins, mitochondria inside healthy cells would more easily recover their ∆ψ, enabling multiple turnovers of PCP import.
claims.source: It is certainly conceivable that the acute addition of saturating quantities of PCP to isolated mitochondria, deployed here, overwhelms their ability to recover ∆ψ. The demand on the import apparatus in vivo would be lower. With sub-saturating levels of precursor proteins, mitochondria inside healthy cells would more easily recover their ∆ψ, enabling multiple turnovers of PCP import.
claims.evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the in vivo situation based on the experimental observations.

claims.claim: PCPs bind only to TIM23 complexes containing two Tim23 subunits and during transport this dimeric organisation becomes disrupted.
claims.source: PCPs bind only to TIM23 complexes containing two Tim23 subunits and during transport this dimeric organisation becomes disrupted (Bauer et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claims.claim: PCP-induced loss of ∆ψ in isolated mitochondria would prohibit the resetting of the TIM23 complex required for further turnovers.
claims.source: Therefore, PCP-induced loss of ∆ψ in isolated mitochondria would prohibit the resetting of the TIM23 complex required for further turnovers.
claims.evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the requirement for ∆ψ in TIM23 dimerisation.

claims.claim: The transfer of PCPs from TOM to TIM23 is thought to involve cooperative interactions of subunits of the two complexes.
claims.source: The transfer of PCPs from TOM to TIM23 is thought to involve cooperative interactions of subunits of the two complexes (Gomkale et al., 2021; Callegari et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: PCPs have been captured spanning both TOM and TIM23 complexes at the same time in super-complexes of ~600 kDa.
claims.source: PCPs have been captured spanning both membrane complexes at the same time in super-complexes of ~600 kDa (Gomkale et al., 2021; Dekker et al., 1997; Gold et al., 2014; Chacinska et al., 2010), suggesting that import through TOM does not have to be complete before import through TIM23 can begin.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: The in vivo existence of TOM-TIM23 super-complexes is unconfirmed.
claims.source: Contrasting with this, however, there is also evidence to suggest that the TOM and TIM23 complexes can transport PCPs independently in steps that are not necessarily concurrent. The in vivo existence of TOM-TIM23 super-complexes is unconfirmed; they have been detected only when engineered PCPs with C-terminal domains that cannot pass through TOM are used (Chacinska et al., 2003), and only under these artificial conditions do TOM and TIM23 subunits co-immuno-precipitate or co-migrate on native polyacrylamide gels (Horst et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Direct handover from TOM to TIM23 is not absolutely required for import.
claims.source: Our results confirm that direct handover from TOM to TIM23 is not absolutely required for import.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the mitoplast experiments showing import can occur without the OMM.

claims.claim: Import of proteins into mitoplasts shows that TOM and soluble factors in the IMS are dispensable for import through TIM23.
claims.source: Import of proteins into mitoplasts, observed here and previously (Hwang et al., 1989; Ohba and Schatz, 1987; van Loon and Schatz, 1987), shows that TOM and soluble factors in the IMS are dispensable for import through TIM23.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from this study and previous studies.

claims.claim: Transport of a PCP through TOM is reversible and therefore possible in the absence of TIM23 activity.
claims.source: The data here also suggest that transport of a PCP through TOM is reversible and therefore possible in the absence of TIM23 activity.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the effect of valinomycin on k1′ and the proposed kinetic model.

claims.claim: Retro-translocation through TOM to cytosolic proteasomes could serve as a checkpoint to ensure that the TIM23 channel does not get blocked when transport across the IMM is compromised.
claims.source: This could serve as a checkpoint to ensure that the TIM23 channel does not get blocked when transport across the IMM is compromised.
claims.evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the potential function of reversible transport.

claims.claim: Proteins that are reduced or conformationally unstable in the IMS can retro-translocate to the cytosol via TOM40, and the efficiency of this process is relative to protein size.
claims.source: For example, proteins that are reduced or conformationally unstable in the IMS can retro-translocate to the cytosol via TOM40, and the efficiency of this process is relative to protein size (both linear length and 3D complexity); smaller proteins are more efficiently retro-translocated (Bragoszewski et al., 2015).

claims.claim: Under physiological conditions, PINK1 is cleaved in the IMM by PARL, releasing the C-terminal region for release back to the cytosol for proteosomal degradation.

results.result: The NanoLuc assay system is validated for measuring mitochondrial protein import. Matrix 11S concentration ranges from 2.8-7.5 µM, signal amplitude is not limited by 11S concentration, and 11S is correctly localized in the matrix.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C29 are well-supported by Western blotting (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), correlation analysis showing no relationship between 11S levels and signal amplitude (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-C), and digitonin extraction experiments confirming matrix localization (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D). These technical validations establish the assay's reliability.

results.result: Import behaves as largely single turnover under experimental conditions, with only ~20% of signal arising from multiple turnovers. The amount of imported PCP matches TIM23 dimer levels (~8.5-11 pmol/mg mitochondria), and only a tiny fraction of added PCP reaches the matrix.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C37, C89 are strongly supported by MTX-blocking experiments with DHFR-tagged constructs (Figure 2), Western blot quantification (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and concentration-dependence studies (Figure 1D). The convergence of multiple experimental approaches provides robust evidence for single-turnover behavior under these conditions.

results.result: Two major rate-limiting steps define import kinetics: k1' corresponds to transport through TOM (length-dependent, exponential relationship suggesting passive diffusion), and k2' corresponds to MTS engagement with TIM23 (length-independent). Transport through TIM23 is fast and not rate-limiting.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C46, C49-C51, C66 are well-supported by systematic analysis of length and position variants (Figure 3), mitoplast experiments (Figure 5), and perturbation studies with valinomycin and ATP depletion (Figure 4). The exponential length-dependence of k1' (Figure 3D) and lack of effect of pep86 position on kinetics provide strong evidence for the proposed assignments.

results.result: Signal amplitude is inversely correlated with protein length for length variants but not position variants. Shorter proteins accumulate at higher levels in the matrix. All three parameters (amplitude, k1', k2') show concentration dependence with distinct KM values.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C48, C52-C55 are supported by experimental data in Figure 3C-F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1. The differential effects on length vs. position variants provide strong evidence that amplitude reflects successful import rather than technical limitations. The concentration-dependence analysis is appropriately fitted to Michaelis-Menten equations.

results.result: Depletion of Δψ and ATP have distinct effects on import kinetics. Valinomycin (10 nM) substantially reduces Δψ and differentially affects k1' and k2' depending on protein length. ATP depletion reduces amplitude more for longer PCPs but has minimal effects on rate constants.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C64 are well-supported by systematic perturbation experiments (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1). The differential effects of valinomycin vs. ATP depletion on different parameters and protein variants provide strong evidence for distinct roles of these energy sources in the import mechanism.

results.result: k2' primarily represents Δψ-dependent insertion of the pre-sequence through TIM23. Under Δψ depletion, length-dependence of k2' emerges, suggesting Δψ drives transport of the mature domain, not exclusively the MTS.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C69 are supported by the lack of length-dependence of k2' in energized mitochondria (Figure 3C) and emergence of length-dependence under valinomycin treatment (Figure 4A). This is further supported by citation to Schendzielorz et al., 2017. The interpretation is logical and consistent with the data.

results.result: Removal of the OMM by digitonin treatment selectively increases k1' but leaves k2' unchanged, confirming k1' occurs at the OMM and k2' at the IMM. Direct handover from TOM to TIM23 is not absolutely required for import.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C76, C101-C102 are strongly supported by mitoplast experiments (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1). The selective effect on k1' but not k2' provides compelling evidence for the proposed assignments. Respirometry data confirm successful OMM removal. The conclusion is further supported by comparison to previous studies.

results.result: PCP net charge has contrasting effects on import: amplitude is inversely correlated with net charge (negatively charged PCPs reach higher levels), while positively charged PCPs are imported faster. PCPs cause depolarization of Δψ that diminishes with increasing negative charge.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C82 are well-supported by charge variant experiments (Figure 6). TMRM fluorescence measurements directly demonstrate charge-dependent effects on Δψ (Figure 6D). Valinomycin pre-treatment abolishing the charge-amplitude correlation (Figure 6E) provides strong mechanistic evidence. The counterintuitive findings are explained by differential Δψ consumption.

results.result: Effects of length and charge on import kinetics observed with artificial PCPs are validated with native mitochondrial proteins (F1α, F1β, Mrp21, Acp1), confirming the generalizability of findings.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C85 are supported by experiments with native PCPs (Figure 7B). The consistency with artificial PCP results strengthens confidence in the broader applicability of the findings. However, the sample size is limited (n=4 proteins), which somewhat limits the strength of this validation.

results.result: The overall model proposes two major rate-limiting steps (passage through TOM and MTS engagement with TIM23) with rapid initial PCP-TOM binding and rapid passage of mature domain through TIM23.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C88 represent the synthesis of all experimental findings. The model is well-supported by the collective evidence from length/position variants, perturbation studies, mitoplast experiments, and charge variants. The assignments are internally consistent and explain the observed kinetic behavior.

results.result: Import is limited by available Δψ under experimental conditions. PCP import causes sustained IMM depolarization that is not restored, and PCPs requiring more energy reach lower final concentrations. The depolarization is a consequence of the import process itself, not mitochondrial dysfunction.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C94 are supported by TMRM measurements (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 2), respirometry data showing mitochondria can build and recover PMF (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, Figure 6—figure supplement 2B), and correlation between PCP properties and amplitude. The evidence distinguishes import-induced depolarization from inherent mitochondrial defects.

results.result: Transport through TOM is reversible and could serve as a checkpoint to prevent TIM23 blockage when IMM transport is compromised.
results.evaluation: Claim C103 is inferred from valinomycin effects on k1' and the kinetic model, but direct evidence for reversibility is limited. Claim C104 is speculative reasoning about potential function. While plausible, these claims require additional experimental validation such as direct observation of retro-translocation under the experimental conditions used.

results.result: In vivo, mitochondria would more easily recover Δψ with sub-saturating PCP levels, enabling multiple turnovers. PCP-induced Δψ loss in isolated mitochondria may prohibit TIM23 complex resetting required for further turnovers.
results.evaluation: Claims C95 and C97 are speculative extrapolations from the experimental observations to the in vivo situation. While the reasoning is logical and based on established knowledge about TIM23 dimerization (C96), these claims lack direct experimental support under physiological conditions. The speculation is reasonable but requires validation.

results.result: NanoLuc formation is faster than ~5 min⁻¹ and will not be resolved by the plate reader. Import kinetics are not affected by matrix 11S concentration variance.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C42 are supported by technical characterization (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B-C) and solution measurements showing NanoLuc formation rate >7.4 min⁻¹. This establishes that NanoLuc formation is not rate-limiting and validates the kinetic analysis approach.

results.result: The concentration dependence of k1' saturates with an apparent KM of 100-200 nM, consistent with initial PCP-TOM association.
results.evaluation: Claim C65 is supported by concentration-dependence data (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1). The KM values are reasonable for protein-protein interactions and consistent with the proposed mechanism involving rapid binding equilibrium followed by slower transport.

results.result: Position variants show no systematic difference in concentration dependence, further supporting that TIM23 passage is not rate-limiting.
results.evaluation: Claim C56 is supported by experimental data (Figure 3F). This finding is consistent with and reinforces the conclusion from C45-C46 that transport through TIM23 is fast and not rate-limiting.

results.result: In mitochondria, transport initiation is slower with rapid processive transport, contrasting with bacterial Sec system.
results.evaluation: Claim C108 is the main conclusion from this study's experimental data and is well-supported by the kinetic analysis. The comparison to bacteria (C107) provides important context. This represents a key mechanistic insight distinguishing mitochondrial from bacterial protein transport.

results.result: Background knowledge about mitochondrial structure, protein import pathways, TOM and TIM23 complexes, and the roles of Δψ and ATP in import.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C9-C23 represent established knowledge in the field, appropriately cited and used to provide context for the experimental work. These are not novel findings but necessary background information.

results.result: The NanoLuc import assay has been previously validated as Δψ-dependent, affected by ATP depletion, and sensitive to TIM23 inhibitors.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C26 cite previous validation work (Pereira et al., 2019) establishing the assay's specificity for TIM23-dependent import. This provides important context for interpreting the current results.

results.result: Previous work showed signal amplitude can be reduced by Δψ depletion, suggesting energy limits import. Channel resetting may require TIM23 dimerization and additional energy input.
results.evaluation: Claim C38 is supported by citation to previous work. Claim C39 is an inference that is reasonable but not definitively proven. Claim C40 is speculative, based on previous reports of TIM23 dimerization but lacking direct experimental evidence in this study. The speculation is plausible but requires validation.

results.result: Background knowledge about TOM-TIM23 interactions, super-complexes, retro-translocation, PINK1 processing, and bacterial Sec system for comparison.
results.evaluation: Claims C96, C98-C100, C105-C107 represent established knowledge from the literature, appropriately cited and used to contextualize the findings and discuss alternative models. These provide important framework for interpreting the results.

results.result: Speculative interpretations about the biological significance of rapid TIM23 transport for mitochondrial fitness and evolutionary pressures on mitochondrial vs. bacterial transport systems.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C109-C110 are speculative reasoning about functional significance and evolutionary pressures. While plausible and logically argued, these claims lack direct experimental support and represent hypotheses for future investigation rather than demonstrated findings.
